messages.subject: Sum of Independent Gamma Random Variables within Multistate Model
parts:
Hello Stan Users,

I'm trying to do something which seems like it should be relatively simple, but is turning out to be nigh impossible (at least with my skillset). First some context: We (USGS Columbia River Research Lab) are working on implementing a multi-state mark recapture model in Stan to estimate survival and transition probabilities (between different migration routes) for individually marked fish migrating through a rather complicated river system. As part of a our multistate model we are interested in amount of time it takes a fish to transit the system depending on the route it takes. So for example consider the following ASCII schematic: 

                      2           3
           A_____|______|__
       1  /                              \     4
R----|--                                 ----|
           \_____|______|___/
          B

A group of fish are released all at the same time at point R on the left-hand side of the schematic. They migrate towards the right. If they are detected at a station (denoted by  "|") their time of passage is detected. After station 1, fish encounter an intersection where they can take either path A or path B. These paths merge back together shortly after each path's respective station 3. We are interested in the distribution of travel times between each station. For example we want to know the mean travel time from R -> 1, from  1 -> 2A or 1->2B, 2A->3A, etc. If we had perfect detection at each station this wouldn't be a problem, but of course we don't. FIsh can pass a station or multiple stations without being detected. But for simplicity lets imagine that no fish die, all fish migrate downstream, and detection at station 4 (the last station) is perfect. So now let's consider three fish, Annie, Billy, and Pat. Annie is detected at station 1, 2A, 3A, and 4 and has the following travel times: R->1 = 1, 1->2A =  2 (cumulative 3), 2A -> 3A = 2 (cumulative 5), and 3A -> 4 = 1 (cumulative 6) days respectively. Billy  is detected at station 1, 2B, 3B, and 4 with travel times of 0.75, 4 (4.75), 4 (8.75), 2 (10.75). Pat on the other hand is detected only at station 1 and station 4 with a travel time of R -> 1 = 1.25 and 1 -> 4 of 7.75 (cumulative 9). So the question is what is the probability model for these travel times?

If these were nice independent Guassian fish, this wouldn't be a problem at all. For Annie we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2A ~ N(mu_2A, sigma_2A), 2A->3A ~ N(mu_3A, sigma_3A), 3A->4 ~ N(mu_4A, sigma_4A). For Billy we have R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1), 1->2B ~ N(mu_2B, sigma_2B), 2B->3B ~ N(mu_3B, sigma_3B), 3B->4 ~ N(mu_4B, sigma_4B). Pat is just a little bit more complicated with R->1 ~ N(mu_1, sigma_1) and 1->4 ~ pA * N(mu_2A + mu_3A + mu_4A, sigma_2A + sigma_3A + sigma_4A) + (1-pA) * N(mu_2B + mu_3B + mu_4B, sigma_2B + sigma_3B + sigma_4B), where pA is the probability of going through route A. But this isn't a problem. It's just a mixture distribution and Stan does great with mixture distributions. I can figure out how to implement and wrap it up together using the forward algorithm within a comprehensive multistate model.

With me so far? Here's the problem: these aren't nice independent Gaussian fish. The travel times we observe are of course all non-negative, but they are also right skewed. So lognormal or gamma are the obvious choices here. Well no big deal right? In order to marginalize everything and get the likelihood for the mixture distribution that describes Pat's cumulative travel time we just need the pdf of the sum of lognormals or gammas. That's where I run into trouble. There is no closed-form pdf for the sum of lognormals. I also don't think I can do imputation because I don't see a way to do that within the mixture distribution framework and keep track of the state when imputing more than one travel time.

So that led me to attempt to implement a model for the sum of independent gammas (different alpha and beta, it's trivial if beta is the same) for which there is a closed form pdf. Paper attached. 

Ok so after all that and before I get into my specific programming question let me lay out my goals for this post. I am primarily interested only in determining mean travel time for each station-to-station segment within a multistate model where I know travel-times are non-negative and right-skewed and where sometimes all I observe are cumulative travel times over multiple segments. I am not married to sum of independent gammas as the solution to this problem, but I latched onto it because I'm fairly certain I need some closed form pdf for the sum of travel times when all I observe is a cumulative travel time.

So onto the distribution of the sum of independent gamma random variables. The problem is that the pdf involves an infinite series. I went ahead an coded up some functions following the Moschopolous paper. The functions take a parameter "m", which is the number of terms of the series to use in approximating the log-likelihood.

I was able to verify that I've coded up the math correctly by specifying some arbitrarily selected values of shape and scale within the generated quantities step and comparing the log-likelihood to the log of empirical density function from a simulation in R. Here's what I noticed, the computation time for a single log-likelihood value for the infinite series as I've coded up increases at a rate of 2^m. For example I investigated the case of the sum of three gamma random variables [beta is rate parameter per Stan's parameterization] X1 ~ Gamma(2, 0.25), X2 ~ Gamma(2.5, 0.5), X3 ~ Gamma(3, 0.75), Y = X1 + X2 + X3.

In R I approximated the log of the empirical density for an arbitrary value as follows:

N = 10000000
alpha = c(2, 2.5, 3)
beta  = c(1/0.25, 1/0.5, 1/0.75)
x = matrix(rep(NA, 3*N), ncol = 3)

x[,1] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[1], scale = beta[1])
x[,2] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[2], scale = beta[2])
x[,3] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[3], scale = beta[3])

Y = rowSums(x)
df = approxfun(density(Y))
plot(density(Y))

log(df(15))

Which for one run gives the following log likelihood:
[1] -2.751022

I compared this value to what I get from the Moschopolous equations in Stan using the generated quantities block with different values of m:

stan_dat = list(N = N,
                m = 25)

s = stan("sum_of_gammas_Moschopoulos.stan", 
         data = stan_dat, 
         chain = 1,
         iter = 1, algorithm = "Fixed_param")

############### y = 15 ##################
#log(df(15)) = -2.751022 #N = 10000000

#m = 10
#log likelihood: -2.76204
#0 seconds 

#m = 15
#log likelihood: -2.75094
#0.06 seconds 

#m = 20
#log likelihood: -2.75084
#1.929 seconds 

#m = 25
#log likelihood: -2.75084
#62.881 seconds 

 So the two things to notice are that 1) at least for this value, the series converged fairly quickly to what I believe is the true value (-2.75084), 2) computation time for a iteration of a single value is approximately 2^(-19 + m) seconds.

Things are less encouraging for value near the right hand tail of the empirical density:
############### y = 40 ##################
#log(df(40)) = -6.652416

#m = 10
#log likelihood: -8.60141
#0 seconds 

#m = 15
#log likelihood: -7.24432
#0.077 seconds 

#m = 20
#log likelihood: -6.76444
#2.031 seconds 

#m = 25
#log likelihood: -6.65741
#64.137 seconds 

So it seems like we need m =  25 to get close to what is probably the true value. But that's 60 seconds for a single iteration of a single log-likelihood value. That's a non-starter.

Undaunted, I attempted to fit simulated data (R code below, Stan code attached) with a fairly low value value of m. But I got nowhere. Stan is telling me that "Gradient evaluated at the initial value is not finite." And I'm not surprised given how poor the approximation seems to be with low values of m.

So I guess my question is whether there is a way to fit the Moschopolous pdf in Stan. Or is there another way to get at the parameters of independent gammas (or lognormals) when sometimes we only observe the sum (without using imputation)? Like I said at the start this seems like it should be simple, but it's most definitely not.

R code to simulate data to fit the model as outlined in the attached Stan code:


N = 1000
p = c(0.75, 0.75, 1)
alpha = c(2, 2.5, 3)
beta  = c(1/0.25, 1/0.5, 1/0.75)
y = matrix(rep(NA, 3*N), ncol = 3)
x = matrix(rep(NA, 3*N), ncol = 3)

x[,1] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[1], rate = beta[1])
x[,2] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[2], rate = beta[2]) 
x[,3] = rgamma(N, shape = alpha[3], rate = beta[3])

y[,1] = x[,1] * rbinom(N, 1, p[1])
y[,2] = (x[,2] + x[,1]) * rbinom(N, 1, p[2])
y[,3] = (x[,3] + x[,2] + x[,1]) * rbinom(N, 1, p[3])

stan_dat = list(N = N,
                y = y,
                m = 15)

s = stan("sum_of_gammas_Moschopoulos.stan", 
         data = stan_dat, 
         chain = 4,
         iter = 1000)

the ADMB meeting and ISEC last year.

If I may summarize, I'm thinking you want to have

X ~ foo(alpha);

Y ~ bar(beta);

and you only observe Z = (X + Y) and want to estimate alpha and
beta? I don't know how to do this in general, other than to have
a latent variable for X for each observation

data {
real Z[N];

parameters {
real X[N];
}
model {
X ~ foo(alpha);
(Z - X) ~ bar(beta);
}

I don't know how to do this in general. Obviously, you'd need to respect
other constraints, but that can be tricky with our language---it won't let
you put varying constraints on parameter vectors, so you need to do the
transform and Jacobian by hand. Suppose you need X and Y to
both be positive and Z is positive. Then you'd have

parameters {
real X_raw[N];
...
transformed parameters {
real X[N] = inv_logit(X) .* Z; // X[n] now in (0, Z[n])
...

model {
// log Jacobian of X_raw -> X transform
target += Z .* log_inv_logit(X) + log1m_inv_logit(X);

- Bob

Thanks Bob,

Yes, we work on some pretty challenging models here. Our shop has gone almost 100% Bayesian because of it. But we're also hitting the limits of JAGS. We have a version of this model coded up in JAGS, but it takes about 4 weeks to run. So we're definitely interested in trying to fit more of these models in Stan. We've actually got our first two papers featuring Stan in the works right now.

After perusing the mailing list yesterday, I think I've come to realize that we're dealing with the convolution of multiple random variables. It sounds like we might have to wait for the fast Fourier transforms to be implemented to try to do the numerical integration. For now, I think my two choices are either to use the Normal distribution which would allow us to account for correlation but not right-skew or strict non-negativity or to use the Gamma distribution with a common rate parameter and assume independence of travel times. We're going to move forward with the Gamma distribution because it's better than what we've got in JAGS.

Just to clarify using your notation below: sometimes we observe only Z, but for some individuals we observe both X and Y. To speak to your suggestions, I don't think the latent variable approach will work within a general multi-state framework. There are two related reasons for this. First, we have to keep track of the number of unobserved travel times because I've discovered Stan does not like imputing a variable that will not be used later. Second, I don't see a way to work with multiple latent variables within a multistate model.

I got as far as figuring out how to do the latent variable approach within a simple three-occasion, three state model (based off the BPA example code on the Stan github page). That code is attached. In the model, I assume that travel time from occasion to occasion is simply based on what the state the individual was in during the last occasion.

The key addition to the basic multistate model is:

  miss_count = 1;

  for (i in 1:N) {
    if (y[i,2] != 3){
      obs_cuml_trav_time[i,2] ~ lognormal(mu[y[i,1]], sigma[y[i,1]]);
      if (y[i,3] !=3){
        real diff;
        diff = obs_cuml_trav_time[i,3] - obs_cuml_trav_time[i,2];
        diff ~ lognormal(mu[y[i,2]], sigma[y[i,2]]);
      } 
    } else { //y[i,2] == 3
      if (y[i,3] !=3){
        real diff;
        tt_1_missing[miss_count] ~ lognormal(mu[y[i,1]], sigma[y[i,1]]);
        diff = obs_cuml_trav_time[i,3] - tt_1_missing[miss_count];
        miss_count = miss_count + 1;
        if (y[i,1] == 1)
          target += log_sum_exp(log(1 - psiAB[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[1], sigma[1]), //probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
                                log(psiAB[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[2], sigma[2]));//probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
        if (y[i,1] ==2)
          target += log_sum_exp(log(psiBA[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[1], sigma[1]), //probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
                                log(1 - psiBA[1]) + lognormal_lpdf(diff | mu[2], sigma[2]));//probability fish was in state 1 during time 2
      }
    }
  }

But this becomes intractable when you get beyond three occasions because we'd need a discrete latent variable to keep track of which state the individual was actually in to avoid impossible sums.

Hey Bob,

Let me try to illustrate my thinking on what I mean by impossible sums appearing when imputing multiple travel times.

Consider the following. We have a 4 occasion capture history with two states (three including death) E.g. AAAB. This capture history is associated with a vector of cumulative travel time Z, with Z[1] = 0, Z[2], = X[1], Z[3] = X[1] + X[2], Z[4] = X[1] + X[2] + X[3]. X[t] is travel time from occasion t to occasion t + 1 and is distributed conditional on the state the individual is in during time t. So under this example X[1] ~ foo(alpha), X[2] ~ foo(alpha), X[3] ~ foo(alpha).

Now consider the capture history AXXB. Here the individual was no observed during the second and third occasion. So Z[2] and Z[3] = NA. All we observe is the final cumulative travel time which is ostensibly the sum of three latent occasion to occasion travel times. We can impute these as follows: 

X[1] ~ foo(alpha) 
X[2] ~ (1 - psiAB[1])*foo(alpha) + psiAB[1]*foo(alpha). 
X[3] ~ (1 - psiAB[1])*(1 - psiAB[2])*foo(alpha) +  (1 - psiAB[1])*(psiAB[2])*bar(beta) + psiAB[1]*psiBA[2]*foo(alpha) + psiAB[1]*(1-psiBA[2])*bar(beta)

But imagine that movement between AB is not possible between occasion 2 and 3. So psiAB[2] = psiBA[2] = 0.

This leaves us with:

 X[3] ~ (1 - psiAB[1])*foo(alpha) +  psiAB[1]*bar(beta)

So let's get arbitrary for illustration purposes and say that foo(alpha) = Uniform(2, 3) and bar(beta) = Uniform(4, 5) (i.e. mutually exclusive). So under this formulation the sum 2.5 + 2.5 + 4.5 would be impossible because that means the individual was in state A during time t = 2, but in state B during time t = 3. But because we have to marginalize out the discrete latent variable (i.e. the unoberved state), nothing prevents Stan from considering this impossible sum, unless we also impute a state variable that effectively forces X[3] ~foo(alpha) if X[2] ~ foo(alpha). I'm under the impression that this is gradient breaking, but maybe I'm wrong?

If the latent states are continuous, you can use parameters
for them and let the MCMC do the marginalization.

The only thing you really have to worry about
is your constraints:

> Z[2] = X[1],

If Z[2] and Z[3] are not observed, but Z[4] is, then
you know:

X[1] + X[2] + X[3] = Z[4]

You can parameterize this many different ways. One

transform and then probably apply a Jacobian depending
on how you're coding up priors.

For my very much simplified example, the basic process is that fish transition among states between discrete occasions and that each occasion is associated with continuous travel time whose distribution is conditional on the state it was in during the previous occasion.

Data
A capture history.  We have four occasions and two states. We condition on all fish being released in state A. Fish can transition between states A and B between occasions 1 and 2, and 3 and 4, but not between 2 and 3. They can die (state U) in between any occasion. Thus, under perfect detection, there are 9 possible capture histories: H  in (AAAA, AAAB, AAAU, ABBA, ABBB, ABBU, AAUU, ABUU, AUUU).  

A cumulative travel time vector. Cumulative travel time since release is recorded at each occasion. Z = (0, Z[2], Z[3], Z[4]). If the fish is dead (or unobserved when we introduce that), an NA is recorded. Station-to-station travel times are derived as the difference between subsequent entries of the travel time vector such that X[1] = Z[2] - 0, X[2] = Z[3] - Z[2], X[3] = Z[4] - Z[3]. It should be obvious, but we can rewrite the cumulative travel time vector as (0, X[1], X[1] + X[2], X[1] + X[2] + X[3]). 

PARAMETERS
For fully observed data, we have the following parameters. 
S_A  = Pr(H(t+1) = U| H(t) = A)
S_B  = Pr(H(t+1) = U| H(t) = B)
psiAB[1] = Pr(H(2) = B |  H(1) = A)
psiAB[3] = Pr(H(4) = B |  H(3) = A)
psiBA[3] = Pr(H(4) = A |  H(3) = B)

Where, S_A = survival from occasion t to t +1 conditional on state being in state A at time t.  Similarly, for S_B. 
and psiAB[1] probability of transitioning to state B from state A between occasion 2 and occasion 1. Similarly, for psiAB[3], psiBA[3]. 

Assuming station-to-station travel times are independently distributed Normal random variables (I DO NOT WANT to assume this for our actual applied example) we also have,
mu_A     = mean travel time for fish in state A during time t.
mu_B     = mean travel time for fish in state B during time t.
sigma_A = standard deviation of travel time for fish in state A during time t
sigma_B = standard deviation of travel time for fish in state B during time t

This is a trivial model with out worrying about unobserved data. We can use the forward algorithm to get the distribution for our capture histories, but some arbitrary examples are:
Pr(AAAB) = S_A*(1-psiAB[1])*S_A*S_A*psiAB[3]
Pr(ABBX) = S_A*psiAB[1]*S_B*(1-S_B)
Pr(AAXX) = S_A*(1-psiAB[1]*(1-S_A)

The associated travel time vectors are also trivial:
For AAAB we have Z[2] = X[1] ~ N(mu_A, sigma_A^2), Z[3] - Z[2] = X[2] ~ N(mu_A, sigma_A^2), Z[4] - Z[3] = X[3] ~ N(mu_A, sigma_A^2).
For ABBU we have Z[2] = X[1] ~ N(mu_A, sigma_A^2), Z[3] - Z[2] = X[2] ~ N(mu_B, sigma_B^2)
For AAUU we have Z[2] = X[1] ~ N(mu_A, sigma_A^2)

If we add in non-detection during occasion 2, 3, and 4 such that fish that are unobserved can be either dead or just not detected we get an additional 12 possible capture histories. (AUAA, AUAB, AUAU, AUBA. AUBB, AUBU, AAUA, AAUB, AAUB, ABUA, ABUB, AUUA, AUUB).

We need to add in detection parameters now - p[2], p[3], p[4] - describing the probability of detection during each occasion. Determining the probability for each capture history becomes more complicated, but we can easily use the forward algorithm. I know how to do this. The issue now is determining the density for observed cumulative travel times for capture history which mean we only observe some elements of Z. 

For example, for capture history AUAU we only observe Z[3]. We know it is the sum of the unobserved X[1] and X[2]. Because we're working with the Normal distribution, we can easily use Z[3] ~ N(mu_A + mu_A, sigma_A^2 + sigma_A^2). This is because we know the fish must have been in state A during occasion 2 given that we know it was in state A during occasion 3. 

The most complicated cases for travel time in this toy example are AUUB and AUUA. In both cases we only observe Z[4] which we know to be the sum of unobserved X[1], X[2], X[3]. But we can still take advantage of the sum of Normals and fit this as a mixture distribution.
